meta.name: The Tie-break (reference)
meta.description: Brand launch for the New Balance x Miu Miu collection with Coco Gauff, told as a playable tennis tie-break. Analysed as the reference for the CafeDuo landing redesign; the goal is to understand why it works, not to copy it.
source_references: https://thetiebreak.merci-michel.com/ (Merci Michel, Awwwards Site of the Day 2026-09-25)
Viewport captures at 1440x900 of intro, rules, countdown, rally, point won and photo reveal (not committed: third-party campaign photography)

color.palette_type: analogous (cool navy and slate taken from the photograph) with one blue accent

primary.role: dominant field: the blurred campaign photo's navy, covers about a quarter of the frame

secondary.role: ink-black shadows of the photo; ground of the intro screens

accent.role: court lines and score on the player's side; under 1% coverage

neutral.usage: #F4F5F8 is the only text colour, always on top of the photo; the greys are photo tones, never UI fills

semantic.success: not observed (a won point is shown by the photo coming into focus, not by colour)

surface.background: #283E6C (full-bleed photograph, never a flat UI colour)
surface.card: none: the site has no cards

color.contrast_strategy: white type and lines over a darkened, blurred photograph; the blur is the scrim

measured_palette.role: warm photo tone (skin, red court line)

typography.font_style_notes: A narrow, high-contrast serif carries every sentence the visitor reads, including the score; the sans appears only on tiny controls. Two families, three sizes in practice: huge, medium and tiny.

spacing.base_unit: court geometry, not a pixel scale: elements sit on the service lines and centre line
spacing.section_rhythm: no sections: one full-screen stage whose state changes (intro, rules, countdown, rally, reveal)

layout.grid_system: a tennis court drawn in perspective is the grid; text centres in the service box
layout.breakpoints: stage scales with the viewport; controls switch from arrow keys to touch

border_radius.pill: only the small round paddles and ball

shape.border_usage: none on UI; the only lines are the court lines, which are the content
shape.divider_style: court lines in white, blue (player) and red (opponent) with a soft glow

elevation.depth_cues: focus: blurred photo behind sharp lines; depth of field is the only depth

iconography.style: almost none: keyboard key glyphs in the rules screen, pause and mute

motion.easing: slow ease-in-out on focus pulls, linear ball physics

duration_scale.macro: about 1.5s focus pull and text cross-fade

motion.entrance_pattern: copy cross-fades in place inside the service box; one sentence at a time
motion.exit_pattern: the previous sentence fades out before the next appears
motion.philosophy: cinematic: the camera (focus) moves, the layout never does

components.button_style: a single small outlined Start, later plain text buttons with an arrow (Next, Click to continue)
components.input_style: the game controls are the input: arrow keys or pointer
components.navigation_pattern: none: the experience is linear, pause and mute are the only chrome
components.modal_style: none: state changes happen on the same stage
components.component_notes: The site has about five DOM elements on top of one WebGL canvas. Everything else is the scene.

aesthetic.visual_metaphor: a tie-break: the decisive moment of a match, played by the visitor
aesthetic.era_influence: 1970s tennis broadcast and film grain, mixed with a modern fashion editorial

visual_language.ornamentation: none: the court lines are function, not decoration
visual_language.whitespace_usage: the photograph fills the space; there is no empty ground
visual_language.contrast_level: medium (soft photo) with high-contrast white text

composition.hierarchy_method: scale contrast between the serif sentence and tiny labels
composition.flow_direction: time, not space: one screen that changes state
composition.grouping_strategy: the court boxes group information (score in a corner of each half)
composition.negative_space_role: the blur acts as negative space while still being a picture

imagery.photo_treatment: full-bleed campaign photography, heavily blurred and grained during play, revealed sharp as a reward
imagery.graphic_elements: court lines with chromatic tint and slight glow

interaction_feel.feedback_style: the scene answers: ball physics, score change, focus pull on a point
interaction_feel.loading_style: the intro screen is the loader
interaction_feel.microinteraction_density: low in the UI, high in the game

brand_voice_in_ui.cta_style: friendly invitation (Start, Next, Click to continue)

overview.fallback_strategy: not observed; the experience depends on WebGL2
overview.primary_technology: WebGL2 with a custom bundle (no global three.js, GSAP or Pixi detected)

background_effects.description: Campaign photograph rendered as a full-screen texture, blurred during play and pulled into focus after a point

3d_elements.description: A court drawn in perspective over the photo, with a ball and two paddles; the camera stays fixed

params.interaction_model: arrow keys or pointer move the player's paddle

shader_effects.description: Blur and grain on the photo; the blur radius is the game's reward signal

scroll_morphing.description: the page does not scroll; progress is driven by play

cursor_effects.description: the pointer steers the paddle instead

image_effects.description: Blur-to-focus reveal of a sharp product photograph after each point

canvas_drawings.description: court lines and score drawn into the same canvas as the photo

params.color_scheme: white, #4A79D8 player side, red opponent side

visual_effects.composite_notes: Three layers: a grained, blurred photo; an emissive court whose lines double as the layout grid; a few DOM sentences in Instrument Serif. Winning a point pulls the photo into focus and pauses on the sharp campaign image with Click to continue. The game is the navigation: the visitor never scrolls. Type sizes were measured from computed styles; the court and focus behaviour were observed from captures and are approximate.
